title: Social Movements and Activism
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about how ordinary people, organising together, have reshaped laws and attitudes -- from the civil rights marches to the hashtags of today.
competenceGoals: analyze the role of social movements in creating social and political change
compare historical and contemporary forms of activism in English-speaking countries
evaluate the effectiveness of different strategies for social change

content.content:
## How ordinary people change the world

Almost every freedom you take for granted was, at some point, considered impossible. The abolition of slavery, votes for women, civil rights, marriage equality -- none of these were handed down from above. Each was won by ordinary people who organised, persisted and refused to accept that things had to stay as they were. The engine of that change has a name: the **social movement**.

A social movement is an organised, sustained effort by a group of people to promote or resist social change. It differs from a one-off protest in several ways: it is *collective*, involving groups acting together; *sustained*, persisting over time; *purposeful*, with identifiable goals; *contentious*, challenging existing power and often facing resistance; and *identity-forming*, giving participants a shared sense of purpose. Movements tend to emerge when three conditions line up: a widely felt **grievance** (injustice or deprivation), a political **opportunity** (the freedom to organise and sympathetic allies), and **resources** (leadership, networks, communication and funding). When all three are present, change becomes possible.

## The strategies that work, and a movement that proved it

Movements come in types and use a toolkit of strategies. A **reform movement** seeks to change specific parts of society, like the campaign for marriage equality; a **revolutionary movement** seeks deep transformation, like the anti-apartheid struggle in South Africa; a **resistance movement** seeks to prevent or reverse change. Their tactics include **civil disobedience** -- deliberately and nonviolently breaking an unjust law while accepting the legal consequences, a method linked to Thoreau, Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr. -- as well as **nonviolent resistance** through boycotts, sit-ins, marches and strikes, **direct action** beyond conventional channels, and **grassroots organising** built from local communities upward. Notably, research shows that nonviolent campaigns are historically *more* successful than violent ones.

The American Civil Rights Movement of 1954 to 1968 is perhaps the clearest demonstration of these strategies working together. After the abolition of slavery in 1865, Black Americans in the South lived under Jim Crow laws -- segregation enforced by law and by violence, denying the vote, equal education and basic dignity. The movement fought back on multiple fronts. It pursued **legal challenges** through the NAACP, winning *Brown v. Board of Education* in 1954, which ruled school segregation unconstitutional. It used **nonviolent direct action** -- the Montgomery Bus Boycott, the Greensboro sit-ins, the Freedom Rides, the March on Washington and the Selma marches. It practised **moral persuasion**, deliberately exposing the brutality of segregation to national television audiences, turning peaceful protesters attacked by fire hoses and police dogs into a force for change. It built **coalitions** across racial, religious and political lines, and applied **legislative pressure** that produced the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Yet the movement's own story carries an honest lesson: it transformed law and culture but did not erase racial inequality, which persists in wealth, education, health and justice -- proof that legal change alone cannot undo centuries of structural injustice.

content.content:
## Activism in the age of the hashtag

The rise of social media has transformed how movements organise, and modern campaigns show both its power and its limits. **Black Lives Matter**, founded in 2013 after the acquittal in the killing of Trayvon Martin, grew into a global movement after the murder of George Floyd in 2020, using social media to organise, document police violence and share personal stories through a decentralised structure of local chapters -- and it sparked what may be the largest protest movement in American history. **Fridays for Future**, begun by Swedish teenager Greta Thunberg protesting alone outside parliament, spread worldwide through social media into mass school strikes for the climate, showing how individual action can ignite collective movements. **#MeToo**, popularised in 2017 and building on activist Tarana Burke's earlier work, used social media to reveal how widespread sexual harassment and assault really are, amplifying voices long silenced.

Digital activism has real strengths: rapid mobilisation that can scale from local to global in days, low barriers so anyone with a phone can take part, instant documentation of abuses, and global solidarity across borders. But it has real weaknesses too, and a balanced view holds both. Critics warn of **slacktivism** -- low-effort online gestures like liking or sharing that may substitute for meaningful action. Filter bubbles can limit exposure to opposing views; the constant stream of outrage can cause burnout; governments can use the same platforms for surveillance and suppression; and online movements can lose momentum as quickly as they gain it. The most effective modern movements tend to combine digital tools with traditional organising. And as **backlash** -- organised resistance from those who feel threatened -- reminds us, social change is rarely quick or complete. Even successful movements face unfinished agendas and pushback, which is part of why activism remains a long, demanding form of citizenship rather than a single viral moment.

questions.task: How did Fridays for Future begin?

options.text: With Greta Thunberg protesting alone outside the Swedish parliament

questions.solution: Fridays for Future began with Swedish teenager Greta Thunberg striking from school alone, before spreading worldwide through social media.

options.text: A highly effective form of protest
Low-effort online activism that may substitute for meaningful action

questions.solution: Slacktivism is a critical term for low-effort online activism, such as liking or sharing, that may make people feel involved without producing real change.

questions.task: Which is a genuine strength of digital activism?

options.text: It removes the need for any organising
Rapid mobilisation and low barriers to participation
It is immune to government surveillance

questions.solution: Digital activism enables rapid mobilisation, low barriers to participation, instant documentation and global solidarity -- though it has weaknesses too.

questions.task: What does "backlash" refer to in the study of social movements?

options.text: Organised resistance from those who feel threatened by change

questions.solution: Backlash is organised resistance to social change, often from those who feel threatened by a movement's goals, and can take political, cultural or violent forms.

content.content:
## In short

Social movements -- organised, sustained, collective efforts to promote or resist change -- have been the main engine of progress in history, emerging when grievance, opportunity and resources come together. The American Civil Rights Movement showed the power of legal challenges, nonviolent direct action, moral persuasion and coalition-building, while honestly reminding us that legal victories did not erase deep inequality. Modern movements like Black Lives Matter, #MeToo and Fridays for Future harness digital tools for speed, scale and global reach, but face real weaknesses -- slacktivism, filter bubbles, burnout and surveillance. The most effective combine digital and traditional methods, and all of them encounter backlash, because change is rarely quick or complete.
